subject: Medicine
summary: Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) is a life‑threatening diabetic emergency with extreme hyperglycaemia, high plasma osmolality, severe dehydration and minimal ketosis, usually in older type‑2 diabetics.

sections.p: HHS is defined by plasma glucose >30 mmol/L (≈540 mg/dL), serum osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, profound dehydration, and absent or mild ketosis. Diagnosis requires excluding diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA).
b: Glucose >30 mmol/L
Osmolality >320 mOsm/kg
Ketones negative or <0.6 mmol/L
Effective serum bicarbonate usually >18 mmol/L

sections.p: Severity is graded by the degree of dehydration, osmolality, and neurologic status. Mild (dehydration <5 %), moderate (5‑10 %), severe (>10 % or coma).
b: Mild: osmolality 320‑350 mOsm/kg, alert
Moderate: osmolality 350‑400 mOsm/kg, confusion
Severe: osmolality >400 mOsm/kg, seizures/coma

sections.p: Any precipitant that raises glucose or worsens dehydration can trigger HHS. In low‑resource settings infections are common triggers.
b: Infection (pneumonia, urinary tract, sepsis, TB, malaria)
Poor oral intake or vomiting
New or stopped glucose‑lowering drugs
Acute stroke or myocardial infarction
Use of corticosteroids or sympathomimetics

sections.p: Patients develop progressive polyuria, polydipsia, and weight loss over days, then present with lethargy, dehydration, and sometimes focal neurologic signs.
b: Dry mucous membranes, poor skin turgor
Weak pulse, tachycardia
Altered mental status ranging from confusion to coma

sections.p: Laboratory and bedside tests confirm hyperglycaemia, osmolality, and rule out ketosis.

t.b: Is hyperglycaemia severe enough for HHS? >30 mmol/L confirms diagnosis
Is plasma osmolality >320 mOsm/kg? Indicates severe dehydration and risk of cerebral edema
Are ketones present? Minimal/absent supports HHS, high levels suggest DKA
What is the degree of dehydration and electrolyte disturbance? Guides fluid replacement
Is there metabolic acidosis? Bicarbonate >18 mmol/L favours HHS
Is an infection present? Identifies precipitating cause
Are there potassium or calcium abnormalities? Detects cardiac risk before fluid shifts

sections.p: Without rapid treatment, HHS can cause cerebral edema, thromboembolic events, and multi‑organ failure.
b: Severe neurologic decline (seizures, coma)
Rapid rise in serum sodium (>160 mmol/L)
Signs of myocardial ischemia or arrhythmia
Acute kidney injury

sections.p: Treat the precipitating cause, then replace fluids, correct electrolytes, and lower glucose gradually. Monitor vitals, glucose, and electrolytes closely.
b: IV isotonic saline 0.9% to restore intravascular volume (first 1‑2 L unless cardiac failure)
Switch to 0.45% saline once corrected sodium approaches normal
Add IV insulin infusion after initial fluid resuscitation; low dose to avoid rapid osmolar shifts
Replace potassium once serum K⁺ >3.3 mmol/L; monitor hourly
Treat infection with appropriate antibiotics; consider antimalarial or anti‑TB therapy where relevant

sections.p: After acute recovery, optimise diabetes control, educate on sick‑day rules, and arrange regular monitoring.
b: Review oral hypoglycaemic regimen or insulin dose
Teach patients to check glucose and hydrate during illness
Schedule early outpatient review within 1‑2 weeks

sections.p: Conditions that share hyperglycaemia or altered mental status can be mistaken for HHS.
b: Diabetic ketoacidosis – prominent ketosis, lower glucose
Hyperglycaemic crisis due to medication overdose – may have similar labs but different trigger
Septic encephalopathy – infection without extreme hyperglycaemia

sections.p: Certain lab values may appear normal despite severe disease.
b: Serum sodium may be falsely low (pseudohyponatraemia) due to hyperglycaemia; correct using glucose‑adjusted formula
Bicarbonate can be normal early, masking evolving acidosis
Ketone strips may miss low‑level ketonaemia; use β‑hydroxybutyrate assay if doubt

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain or shortness of breath suggesting cardiac ischemia

faq.q: Why is ketosis minimal in HHS?
faq.a: Residual insulin suppresses lipolysis, so glucose rises without the massive fatty‑acid breakdown that produces ketones.

faq.q: Can HHS occur in type 1 diabetes?
faq.a: Rarely, because type 1 patients usually lack enough insulin to prevent ketosis, leading to DKA instead.

faq.q: What is the most important immediate therapy?
faq.a: Aggressive isotonic fluid replacement to restore perfusion and reduce plasma osmolality.

exam: List the diagnostic criteria for HHS and explain how they differ from DKA.
Describe the step‑wise fluid management plan for a patient with severe HHS.
Identify three common precipitating factors for HHS in low‑resource settings and how they influence treatment.
